gloss: Control or authority over people or land.
examples: The empire held *dominion* over most of the region.
They believed humans had *dominion* over nature.
The king lost *dominion* over the northern provinces.

gloss: A small device that plugs into a computer to add a connection or unlock software.
examples: You'll need a *dongle* to connect the projector to your laptop.
I lost the *dongle* that came with the wireless mouse.
The new laptops need *dongles* for everything.

gloss: A terrible fate that cannot be avoided.
examples: A sense of *doom* hung over the whole town.
The news channel is nothing but *doom* and gloom.
He walked toward his *doom* without saying a word.

gloss: The vertical post on either side of a doorway.
examples: He leaned against the *doorjamb* and watched us cook.
We marked the kids' heights on the *doorjamb*.
The *doorjambs* were painted a different color than the walls.
contrast: The final b is silent: DOR-jam.

gloss: A person who looks exactly like someone else.
examples: I saw your *doppelganger* at the airport this morning.
The actor met his *doppelganger* at a fan convention.
Twins aside, most people never meet their *doppelgangers*.

gloss: A period when a plant, animal, or process is inactive.
examples: The bulbs need a few months of *dormancy* before they bloom.
The virus can stay in *dormancy* for years.
Winter *dormancy* protects the tree from frost.

gloss: A building where students live at a college or school.
examples: She spent her first year in a *dormitory* on campus.
The *dormitories* are closed over winter break.
Our *dormitory* had a shared kitchen on every floor.

gloss: A collection of documents about a person or subject.
examples: The agency kept a thick *dossier* on every suspect.
She handed the lawyer a *dossier* of emails.
Reporters obtained *dossiers* from the leaked archive.

gloss: A person who takes an actor's place in dangerous or difficult scenes.
examples: The fight scene was filmed with a stunt *double*.
She used a *double* for the horseback riding.
The *doubles* rehearsed the crash for two days.

gloss: A short round rod of wood or metal used to join two pieces together.
examples: The shelf is held together with glue and wooden *dowels*.
Drill a hole and tap the *dowel* in with a mallet.
I bought a *dowel* at the hardware store to fix the chair.

gloss: The loss of someone's power, position, or success.
examples: Greed led to the CEO's *downfall*.
The scandal caused his political *downfall*.
Overconfidence has been the *downfall* of many strong teams.

gloss: A move to a lower level, rank, or rating.
examples: The credit *downgrade* rattled investors.
Moving to a smaller office felt like a *downgrade*.
The airline offered refunds for seat *downgrades*.

gloss: A fall in business activity or in the economy.
examples: Sales dropped sharply during the *downturn*.
The company survived two major *downturns*.
Economists expect a mild *downturn* next year.

gloss: Money or property a bride's family gives to her husband at marriage.
examples: Her family could not afford a *dowry*.
The custom of paying a *dowry* is illegal there now.
*Dowries* appear constantly in nineteenth-century novels.

gloss: The force of air or water that slows down a moving object.
examples: The new body design reduces *drag* at high speeds.
Cyclists ride close together to cut down on *drag*.
Air *drag* is what slows the parachute.

gloss: An imaginary animal like a huge lizard that breathes fire.
examples: The knight fought a *dragon* in the story.
Lunar New Year parades feature enormous paper *dragons*.
My son drew a *dragon* with green wings.

gloss: Someone or something that attracts a lot of people.
examples: The free concert was a big *draw* for families.
Cheap flights are the main *draw* of that airport.
The museum's new exhibit is a real *draw*.

gloss: A disadvantage of something that is otherwise good.
examples: The only *drawback* is the long commute.
Every plan has its *drawbacks*.
Cost is the biggest *drawback* to solar panels.

gloss: A bridge that can be raised to let boats pass or to block entry.
examples: The castle's *drawbridge* was raised at sunset.
We waited ten minutes for the *drawbridge* to come down.
Two *drawbridges* cross the river downtown.

gloss: A slow way of speaking in which the vowels are stretched out.
examples: You can hear a slight Texas *drawl* when he's tired.
She answered in a lazy *drawl*.
Their *drawls* gave away where they grew up.

gloss: Someone whose hopes and ideas are not very practical.
examples: My brother is a *dreamer*, not a planner.
The world needs *dreamers* as well as engineers.
She was called a *dreamer* until the company took off.

gloss: Slow movement caused by wind, water, or a current.
examples: The boat's *drift* carried it toward the rocks.
Continental *drift* explains the shape of the coastlines.
Wind *drift* made the shot miss by a foot.

gloss: Someone who drinks alcohol, especially regularly.
examples: He's a heavy *drinker* and everyone knows it.
Even moderate *drinkers* face some health risks.
She's not much of a *drinker*.

gloss: Saliva that runs out of someone's mouth.
examples: The baby's shirt was soaked with *drool*.
There was *drool* on my pillow when I woke up.
Wipe the *drool* off the dog's chin.

gloss: A very small drop of liquid.
examples: *Droplets* of rain covered the windshield.
The virus spreads through tiny *droplets* in the air.
A single *droplet* of oil floated on the water.

gloss: Hard, boring work that has to be done.
examples: Washing dishes by hand is pure *drudgery*.
The software takes the *drudgery* out of bookkeeping.
She left the job to escape the daily *drudgery*.

gloss: Someone who is drunk, or who often gets drunk.
examples: A *drunk* was shouting outside the bar.
The police picked up two *drunks* on Main Street.
He turned into a mean *drunk* after the divorce.

gloss: The state of being drunk.
examples: He was arrested for public *drunkenness*.
The report blamed the crash on *drunkenness*.
*Drunkenness* is no excuse for what he said.
contrast: Spelled with a double n: drunken + ness.

gloss: The state of having little or no moisture.
examples: The *dryness* of the air made my skin itch.
This lotion helps with winter *dryness*.
Farmers are worried about the *dryness* of the soil.

gloss: The process of replacing a film's original speech with another language.
examples: The Spanish *dubbing* on this show is excellent.
I prefer subtitles to *dubbing*.
*Dubbing* the whole series took three months.

gloss: A woman of very high noble rank, or the wife of a duke.
examples: The *duchess* opened the new hospital wing.
Two *duchesses* attended the ceremony.
A photographer followed the *duchess* all afternoon.

gloss: A fight or contest between two people.
examples: The two men fought a *duel* over an insult.
The debate turned into a *duel* between the front-runners.
Their tennis *duels* drew huge crowds.
contrast: Sounds just like dual ("having two parts"), but a duel is a fight.

gloss: The quality of being boring or lacking interest.
examples: The *dullness* of the lecture put half the room to sleep.
Nothing broke the *dullness* of the long drive.
He complained about the *dullness* of small-town life.

gloss: A short bar with a weight at each end, lifted for exercise.
examples: She lifted a twenty-pound *dumbbell* in each hand.
The *dumbbells* are on the rack by the mirror.
Start with a light *dumbbell* until your form is right.
contrast: The b in dumb is silent: DUM-bel.

gloss: A model of a human body, or a fake copy of something.
examples: Crash-test *dummies* showed how the seatbelt performed.
The store window had a *dummy* wearing a winter coat.
The box on the shelf was just a *dummy*.

gloss: A dark underground prison, usually in a castle.
examples: The prisoners were kept in a damp *dungeon*.
We toured the castle's *dungeons*.
The game's first level is a *dungeon* full of traps.

gloss: An exact copy of something.
examples: Keep the original and mail me a *duplicate*.
I found two *duplicates* of the same photo.
The office made a *duplicate* of my key.
contrast: The noun ends in -kuht (DOO-plih-kuht); the verb ends in -kayt (DOO-plih-kayt).

gloss: Threats or force used to make someone do something.
examples: He claims he signed the contract under *duress*.
A confession given under *duress* is not admissible.
The witness testified that she had acted under *duress*.

gloss: A house or other place where someone lives.
examples: The permit covers single-family *dwellings* only.
Archaeologists found a stone *dwelling* under the field.
Each *dwelling* must have a working smoke alarm.

gloss: The way the people or forces in a group act on and change one another.
examples: Family *dynamics* changed after the baby arrived.
The coach studies team *dynamics* closely.
Office *dynamics* can be hard for a newcomer to read.

gloss: A powerful explosive used in mining and demolition.
examples: They used *dynamite* to blast a tunnel through the ridge.
A stick of *dynamite* was found in the old shed.
*Dynamite* was invented in the 1860s.

gloss: A person who is full of energy and gets a lot done.
examples: Our new manager is a real *dynamo*.
She's a *dynamo* on the sales floor.
The team is full of young *dynamos*.

gloss: A serious infection of the bowels that causes severe diarrhea.
examples: *Dysentery* spread quickly through the camp.
He caught *dysentery* from contaminated water.
Clean water sharply reduces cases of *dysentery*.

gloss: A failure of something to work the way it should.
examples: Years of family *dysfunction* left him dreading the holidays.
The tests showed some kidney *dysfunction*.
Voters say they are tired of *dysfunction* in Congress.

gloss: A condition that makes reading and spelling difficult.
examples: He was diagnosed with *dyslexia* in third grade.
*Dyslexia* has nothing to do with intelligence.
The school offers extra support for students with *dyslexia*.

gloss: A strong feeling of unease or dissatisfaction, especially with one's own body.
examples: She described the *dysphoria* she felt as a teenager.
The clinic treats gender *dysphoria*.
Some patients report *dysphoria* as a side effect.

gloss: An imagined society where life is frightening and unjust.
examples: The novel is set in a *dystopia* run by corporations.
Teen fiction is full of *dystopias*.
The film paints a *dystopia* of endless surveillance.

gloss: A disease in which muscles or tissues gradually weaken.
examples: Muscular *dystrophy* runs in his family.
The charity funds research into *dystrophy*.
*Dystrophy* slowly robbed him of his strength.

gloss: A strong wish to do or have something.
examples: His *eagerness* to help was obvious.
She answered with surprising *eagerness*.
The puppy's *eagerness* made everyone laugh.

gloss: A pain inside the ear.
examples: The baby cried all night with an *earache*.
Swimming in the lake gave me an *earache*.
He gets *earaches* every winter.

gloss: A British nobleman ranking below a marquess.
examples: The *earl* opened his gardens to the public.
Several *earls* still sit in the House of Lords.
He inherited the title of *earl* at twenty-two.

gloss: One of a pair of soft covers worn over the ears to keep them warm.
examples: Don't forget your *earmuffs*, it's ten degrees out.
She pulled her *earmuffs* down over her ears.
One *earmuff* fell off somewhere in the snow.

gloss: A person who earns money, especially at a stated level.
examples: Top *earners* pay a higher tax rate.
She was the main *earner* in the household.
Low *earners* qualify for the credit.

gloss: A small speaker worn in or over the ear for listening privately.
examples: Put your *earphones* in if you want to watch the movie.
One *earphone* stopped working after a week.
He wore *earphones* the whole flight.

gloss: The distance within which a voice can be heard.
examples: Don't say that while the kids are within *earshot*.
She waited until he was out of *earshot*.
Two reporters were standing well within *earshot*.

gloss: Dishes and pots made from baked clay.
examples: She serves soup in heavy *earthenware*.
The shop sells handmade *earthenware*.
*Earthenware* chips more easily than porcelain.

gloss: The direction where the sun rises.
examples: The storm is moving toward the *east*.
The mountains lie to the *east* of the city.
In the *east*, the sky was already turning pink.

gloss: A person or animal that eats in a particular way.
examples: My daughter is a picky *eater*.
Pandas are slow *eaters*.
He's a big *eater* but never gains weight.

gloss: The flowing of the tide back out to sea.
examples: The fishing boat left on the *ebb*.
At the *ebb* you can walk out to the sandbar.
The tide's *ebb* uncovered a wide mudflat.

gloss: A very hard black wood from a tropical tree.
examples: The piano's black keys were once made of *ebony*.
He carved the handle from a block of *ebony*.
*Ebony* is dense enough to sink in water.

gloss: An unusual habit or way of behaving.
examples: Everyone tolerated the professor's *eccentricities*.
Collecting doorknobs is a harmless *eccentricity*.
Age had not softened his *eccentricities*.

gloss: A level or rank within an organization.
examples: She reached the upper *echelons* of the company.
The decision was made at the highest *echelon*.
Only the top *echelons* ever saw the report.

gloss: The use of reflected sound to find objects, as bats and dolphins do.
examples: Bats hunt insects using *echolocation*.
Dolphins rely on *echolocation* in murky water.
The lesson explained how *echolocation* works.

gloss: A long pastry filled with cream and topped with chocolate.
examples: She bought two chocolate *eclairs* on the way home.
The bakery's *eclair* is worth the trip.
*Eclairs* don't keep well overnight.

gloss: An expert who studies how money, goods, and jobs work in a society.
examples: *Economists* disagree about the cause of the slowdown.
She's an *economist* at the Federal Reserve.
The *economist* predicted that rates would fall.

gloss: Travel to natural places that tries not to harm them.
examples: *Ecotourism* brings money to the villages near the reserve.
The country markets itself as a hub for *ecotourism*.
Critics say *ecotourism* can still damage fragile habitats.

gloss: A skin condition that causes dry, red, itchy patches.
examples: Cold weather makes her *eczema* worse.
The doctor prescribed a cream for his *eczema*.
*Eczema* often starts in childhood.

gloss: Swelling caused by fluid trapped in the body's tissues.
examples: The medication reduced the *edema* in her ankles.
*Edema* is common late in pregnancy.
He was hospitalized with *edema* in both legs.
contrast: American spelling is edema; the British spelling is oedema.

gloss: An official order given by someone in power.
examples: The king issued an *edict* banning the practice.
Staff grumbled about the new *edict* from headquarters.
Several *edicts* were reversed within a year.

gloss: A teacher, or someone whose profession is education.
examples: *Educators* across the state opposed the budget cuts.
She's a respected *educator* with thirty years of experience.
The award honors one *educator* each spring.

gloss: A change that something causes.
examples: The medicine had no *effect* on the pain.
Scientists study the *effects* of caffeine on sleep.
The new law's *effect* was immediate.
contrast: Effect is the noun (a result); affect is usually the verb (to influence).

gloss: The ability of something to produce the result it is meant to.
examples: The trial measured the vaccine's *efficacy*.
There's little evidence for the drug's *efficacy*.
Researchers questioned the *efficacy* of the program.

gloss: A rough model of a person, often burned as a protest.
examples: Protesters burned an *effigy* of the governor.
Two *effigies* hung from the courthouse steps.
The crowd carried an *effigy* through the square.

gloss: The ability of a material to stretch and then return to its shape.
examples: Skin loses *elasticity* as we age.
The waistband has lost its *elasticity*.
Rubber is prized for its *elasticity*.

gloss: A feeling of great happiness and excitement.
examples: She felt a rush of *elation* when the results came in.
The team's *elation* lasted all week.
His *elation* faded once the bills arrived.

gloss: A small dark purple berry used in syrup, jam, and wine.
examples: She makes syrup from *elderberries* every fall.
The *elderberry* bush by the fence is loaded this year.
*Elderberries* have to be cooked before you eat them.

gloss: A person chosen to cast a formal vote on behalf of voters.
examples: Each state sends *electors* to the Electoral College.
One *elector* refused to vote as pledged.
The *electors* met in December to certify the result.

gloss: The splitting of a substance into parts by passing electricity through it.
examples: *Electrolysis* separates water into hydrogen and oxygen.
The lab demonstrated *electrolysis* with a battery and two wires.
Aluminum is produced by *electrolysis*.

gloss: A mineral or fluid that carries an electric charge in the body or a battery.
examples: Sports drinks replace *electrolytes* lost in sweat.
His blood test showed low *electrolytes*.
The battery's *electrolyte* had leaked.

gloss: Electronic devices, or the branch of technology that makes them.
examples: He studies *electronics* at the community college.
Don't pack *electronics* in your checked luggage.
The store's *electronics* section is upstairs.

gloss: Graceful beauty in appearance, movement, or design.
examples: The room was decorated with quiet *elegance*.
There's a real *elegance* to her solution.
The dress had the *elegance* of an earlier era.

gloss: A poem or song of sorrow, usually for someone who has died.
examples: He wrote an *elegy* for his grandmother.
The collection ends with three *elegies*.
The piece is less a march than an *elegy*.

gloss: The state of meeting the requirements for something.
examples: Check your *eligibility* before you apply.
The rule change affected his *eligibility* for the scholarship.
*Eligibility* depends on income and household size.

gloss: The act of removing something completely.
examples: The plan calls for the *elimination* of all single-use plastics.
Their *elimination* from the tournament came in the first round.
*Elimination* of the tax would cost billions.

gloss: The belief that a small privileged group should lead or be favored.
examples: Critics accused the university of *elitism*.
There's a whiff of *elitism* in the way he talks about food.
The party campaigned against *elitism*.

gloss: A liquid believed to cure illness or bring long life.
examples: The ad promises a magic *elixir* for tired skin.
Alchemists searched for an *elixir* of life.
The shelf was lined with strange *elixirs*.

gloss: Skill in speaking or writing in a powerful, persuasive way.
examples: She argued the case with real *eloquence*.
His *eloquence* won over the jury.
The letter is remembered for its *eloquence*.

gloss: The act of freeing people from slavery or from legal restrictions.
examples: The proclamation led to the *emancipation* of enslaved people.
The chapter covers *emancipation* and its aftermath.
*Emancipation* did not put an end to discrimination.

gloss: A design or object that stands for a group or an idea.
examples: The eagle is the national *emblem*.
Their jackets carry the club's *emblem*.
Both teams changed their *emblems* last season.

gloss: A person or thing that is a perfect example of a quality.
examples: She was the *embodiment* of patience.
The building is the *embodiment* of 1920s optimism.
The two characters are *embodiments* of greed and generosity.

gloss: A blocked blood vessel caused by a clot or an air bubble.
examples: He died of a pulmonary *embolism*.
Long flights slightly raise the risk of an *embolism*.
Two *embolisms* showed up on the scan.

gloss: The act of holding someone closely in your arms.
examples: She held him in a long *embrace*.
They met at the gate and fell into an *embrace*.
Their *embraces* said more than any words could.

gloss: An unborn animal or human in the earliest stage of development.
examples: The clinic freezes *embryos* for later use.
At six weeks the *embryo* is about the size of a pea.
Chicken *embryos* are used to make some vaccines.

gloss: The process of appearing or becoming known.
examples: The *emergence* of streaming changed the industry.
Scientists tracked the *emergence* of a new variant.
Her *emergence* as a leader surprised no one.

gloss: The act of leaving your own country to live in another one.
examples: War drove mass *emigration* from the region.
*Emigration* has left many villages half empty.
The book traces Irish *emigration* to America.
contrast: Emigration is leaving a country; immigration is entering one.

gloss: A Muslim ruler or prince in some Middle Eastern countries.
examples: The *emir* opened the new airport terminal.
Two *emirs* attended the summit.
The *emir* holds most of the country's power.

gloss: A country or region ruled by an emir.
examples: Seven *emirates* formed a federation in 1971.
The *emirate* invested heavily in tourism.
He works in an *emirate* on the Persian Gulf.

gloss: A person sent to deliver a message or to represent a government.
examples: The president sent an *emissary* to the peace talks.
*Emissaries* from both sides met in secret.
She served as an *emissary* to the region for years.
